Deep Dives  深度探索

The future belongs to those who prepare like Dwarkesh Patel
未来属于像 Dwarkesh Patel 那样做好准备的人

How the rising star of podcasting eschews the breadth v. depth dilemma and is quickly becoming known as ‘the new Lex Fridman.’
播客界新星如何避开广度与深度困境，正迅速成为“新的 Lex Fridman”。
By: Shreeda Segan  作者：Shreeda Segan
Photography: Derek Yarra  摄影：Derek Yarra
February 29, 2024  2024 年 2 月 29 日Updated: August 30, 2024  更新日期：2024 年 8 月 30 日

In a world with over five million podcasts, Dwarkesh Patel stands out as an unexpected trailblazer. At just 23 years old, he has caught the attention of influential figures such as Jeff Bezos, Noah Smith, Nat Friedman, and Tyler Cowen, who have all praised his interviews — the latter describing Patel as “highly rated but still underrated!” Through his podcast, he has created a platform that draws in some of the most influential minds of our time, from tech moguls to AI pioneers.
在超过五百万个播客的世界里，德沃克什·帕特尔是一位意想不到的开拓者。年仅 23 岁，他就吸引了杰夫·贝索斯、诺亚·史密斯、纳特·弗里德曼和泰勒·考恩等知名人士的注意，他们都赞扬他的访谈——后者将帕特尔描述为“评价很高但仍然被低估！”通过他的播客，他创建了一个平台，吸引了我们这个时代最具影响力的人物，从科技巨头到人工智能先驱。

But of all the noteworthy parts of Patel’s journey to acclaim, one thing stands out among the rest: just how deeply he will go on any given topic.
但在帕特尔获得声誉的众多显著经历中，有一件事最为突出：他探讨任何特定话题的深度。

“If I do an AI interview where I’m interviewing Demis [Hassabis], CEO of DeepMind, I’ll probably have read most of DeepMind's papers from the last couple of years. I’ve literally talked to a dozen AI researchers in preparation for that interview — just weeks and weeks of teaching myself about [everything].”
“如果我去做一个 AI 访谈，访谈对象是 DeepMind 的 CEO Demis [Hassabis]，我可能会读过 DeepMind 过去几年的大部分论文。为了准备那次访谈，我实际上和十几个 AI 研究人员谈过——那真是几周又几周的自我学习[关于一切]。”

Patel will even try to implement exercises or simulations from the academic papers themselves, sharing how he “implemented a transformer before interviewing Ilya.”
帕特尔甚至会尝试从学术论文中实施练习或模拟，分享他“在面试伊利亚之前就实现了一个 Transformer”的经历。

It’s like ‘Oh my god, I’m just a random college kid. I get to interview this person. So I’m going to spend a week prepping and reading everything that might even be potentially relevant.’
就像“天啊，我只是一个普通的大学学生。我有机会面试这个人。所以我要花一周时间准备并阅读所有可能相关的资料。”

And it would appear the podcaster’s prep-first approach is working. All of Patel’s growth to date has been completely organic. His show has seen guests like a16z founder Marc Andreessen, OpenAI Chief Scientist Ilya Sutskever, and even the now-convicted Sam Bankman-Fried — a roster that has managed to get the show a loyal following. Patel also writes occasionally on Substack. His most recent piece, “Will scaling work?,” explores the AI takeoff question. It was referenced by Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison and recommended by OpenAI ex-interim CEO Emmett Shear.
而且看来播客主先准备再行动的方法是有效的。帕特尔至今的所有成长都是完全有机的。他的节目邀请了 a16z 创始人马克·安德烈森、OpenAI 首席科学家伊利亚·苏茨凯弗，甚至包括已被定罪的萨姆·班克曼-弗里德——这个阵容成功为节目赢得了忠实的追随者。帕特尔偶尔也会在 Substack 上撰写文章。他最近的一篇文章《规模会成功吗？》，探讨了人工智能起飞的问题。这篇文章被 Stripe 联合创始人帕特里克·科利斯引用，并由 OpenAI 前临时 CEO 埃米特·谢尔推荐。

At the end of his recent Substack post, he disclaims “[F]or what it’s worth, my day job is as a podcaster.” But the disclaimer is quickly followed up with “[T]he people who could write a better post are prevented from doing so, either by confidentiality or opportunity cost.”
在他的最新 Substack 文章结尾，他声明“就我而言，我的日常工作是一名播客主。”但声明很快被补充道“那些能写更好文章的人被阻止这样做，要么因为保密协议，要么因为机会成本。”

So the world gets AI analysis from people who can show up, do the prep, and speak freely instead. In other words, the world gets it from Patel.
所以世界从那些能够出现、做好准备并自由发言的人那里获得 AI 分析。换句话说，世界从帕特尔那里获得。

When I speak to him, Patel dials in from his room in a group house in Hayes Valley, San Francisco. He tells me it’s what he can afford through grants like Emergent Ventures. But I know that he’s currently well positioned in the home of the world’s largest concentration of AI startups.
当我与他交谈时，帕特尔从旧金山海耶斯谷的一处集体住房的房间里接入。他告诉我，这是他通过像新兴企业这样的资助项目能够负担得起的。但我知道，他目前正处于世界上最大 AI 创业公司集中地的家中。

Patel only came to America when he was around nine years old, spending his early life in India. His father, a doctor, sought an H1-B visa and was often assigned positions in rural America, where there was demand for quality doctors. Through Patel’s teens, the family shuffled around states like North Dakota, West Virginia, Maryland, and later, Texas, where Patel eventually attended college.
帕特尔九岁左右才来到美国，他的早年生活在印度度过。他的父亲是一名医生，申请了 H1-B 签证，经常被分配到美国农村地区，那里对优质医生有需求。在帕特尔青少年时期，全家辗转于北达科他州、西弗吉尼亚州、马里兰州等地，后来搬到了德克萨斯州，帕特尔最终在那里上了大学。

He graduated from UT Austin in December 2021 with a degree in computer science. It’s where he was taught by professors like Scott Aaronson, the well-known computational complexity theorist and author of Quantum Computing Since Democritus. It’s also where he launched the Lunar Society Podcast from his dorm room on a whim during the heights of the COVID-19 pandemic. It was a time when Patel was feeling particularly intellectually isolated and turned to books for inspiration.
他在 2021 年 12 月从德克萨斯大学奥斯汀分校获得计算机科学学位。在那里，他由像斯科特·阿隆森这样的教授授课，斯科特是著名的计算复杂性理论家，也是《自德谟克利特以来的量子计算》的作者。也是在那里，在 COVID-19 大流行的高峰期，他一时兴起，从宿舍里推出了月球学会播客。那时，帕特尔感到特别孤立，转向书籍寻求灵感。

He was reading The Case Against Education when he cold-emailed author Bryan Caplan to share that he loved his book. To Patel’s surprise, Caplan replied. It was then that Patel decided to “shoot his shot” and ask Caplan for a podcast episode.
当他阅读《反对教育的案例》时，他给作者布莱恩·卡普兰发了封冷邮件，分享他喜欢这本书。令帕特尔惊讶的是，卡普兰回复了。那时，帕特尔决定“放手一搏”，请求卡普兰做一集播客。

“He assumed I had an actual podcast. I didn’t even have a name for a podcast. But he was kind enough, he did it,” says Patel. Caplan became Patel’s first-ever guest.
“他以为我有一个真正的播客。我甚至还没有给播客取名字。但他很友善，他做到了，”帕特尔说。卡普兰成了帕特尔有史以来的第一位嘉宾。

To Patel, it was a big deal. “It’s like ‘Oh my god, I’m just a random college kid. I get to interview this person. So I’m going to spend a week prepping and reading everything that might even be potentially relevant.’”
对帕特尔来说，这是一件大事。“就像‘天啊，我只是一个普通的大学学生。我有机会采访这个人。所以我要花一周时间准备，阅读所有可能相关的资料。’”

Fortunately, the prep paid off. “Caplan enjoyed the podcast so much that he recommended it to Tyler Cowen of GMU. Cowen came on pretty early. From there, it just became something I did on the side while in college.”
幸运的是，准备得到了回报。“Caplan 非常喜欢这个播客，以至于他向 GMU 的 Tyler Cowen 推荐了它。Cowen 很早就加入了。从那时起，它就变成了我在大学期间做的一种副业。”

This level of deep research is, for him, a way of respecting the opportunities he has in being able to speak to highly-regarded figures with influence, despite starting from a place of little influence himself.
对他来说，这种深入的研究是一种尊重他能够与有影响力的人物交谈的机会的方式，尽管他本人起点影响力很小。

Keep the insights coming.
继续分享见解。

Get relevant reads and resources in your inbox, once a month.
每月一次，将相关的阅读和资源发送到您的邮箱。

Today, Patel is quickly becoming known as “the new Lex Fridman” and even “Lex Fridman but better.” Here, again, he credits his success to prep. On Lex Fridman and other competitors, Patel says “Sometimes it doesn’t feel like they’re trying. In other fields, if something is your full-time job, there’s an expectation for you to spend a lot of effort on it. The idea of popular podcasters just walking into a studio after just a single day of prep… It’s like this is your full-time job, man. Why don’t you spend a week or two instead?
如今，帕特尔正迅速被称为“新的莱克·弗里德曼”，甚至“比莱克·弗里德曼更出色”。在这里，他再次将成功归功于准备。对于莱克·弗里德曼和其他竞争对手，帕特尔说：“有时候感觉他们并没有认真尝试。在其他领域，如果这是你的全职工作，人们期望你投入大量精力。那些流行播客的主播只是准备一天就走进录音棚……这就像这是你的全职工作，伙计。你为什么不花上一两周呢？

“Most of the prep I do just doesn’t end up being useful because I’ll have read a random thing that never came up in the conversation. But some of the things I end up reading, even randomly on my own time, lead to interesting conversations.”
“我做的准备大部分最终都没有用，因为我读了一些随机的东西，而这些东西在对话中从未出现。但有些我读的东西，即使是在我自己的时间里随机阅读的，也引出了有趣的对话。”

There is a growing cult following of Patel fans who appreciate this approach. Guests on his podcast might be the same guests that Lex Fridman talks to — guests from a wide range of fields who might also have important insights on technology. But Patel is going to stick only to that guest’s domain, attempting to, in his own words, “80/20 an undergrad course on the topic” before the interview. In this way, the 23-year-old has managed to create his own seat, at his own table, for some of the most important conversations about AI, economy, technology, and history.
帕特尔有一种日益增长的狂热粉丝群体，他们欣赏这种做法。他在播客中的嘉宾可能与莱克斯·弗里德曼访谈的嘉宾相同——来自广泛领域的嘉宾，他们也可能对技术有重要见解。但帕特尔只会专注于那位嘉宾的领域，试图在他自己的话中，“在采访前对主题进行 80/20 的本科课程”。通过这种方式，这位 23 岁的年轻人已经成功为自己在人工智能、经济、技术和历史等一些最重要对话中，创造了属于自己的座位和桌子。

The Pareto principle, also known as the 80/20 rule, states that 80% of the consequences come from 20% of the causes. (It stems from the Pareto distribution, a power-law probability distribution that describes phenomena across a variety of fields.) When applying the Pareto principle to the broader podcasting industry, where a few podcasts achieve significant success over the more than 5 million that exist today according to Forbes, it suggests that a small percentage of podcasts (around 20%) garner a large majority (approximately 80%) of listenership, engagement, and revenue.
帕累托原则，也被称为 80/20 法则，指出 80%的结果来自 20%的原因。（它源于帕累托分布，一种描述跨多个领域现象的幂律概率分布。）当将帕累托原则应用于更广泛的播客行业时，根据福布斯的数据，当今超过 500 万个播客中只有少数播客取得了显著成功，这表明一小部分播客（约 20%）获得了绝大多数（约 80%）的听众、参与度和收入。

This information might discourage most aspiring podcasters from even trying, but it did not discourage Patel. The recent conversation he had with Patrick Collison is top-of-mind for Patel as he shares how the idea of an industry being too crowded, in the first place, is somewhat of a fallacy.
这些信息可能会让大多数有志于播客的人望而却步，但它并没有阻止帕特尔。他与帕特里克·科利森的最近对话一直萦绕在帕特尔心头，因为他分享了关于一个行业从一开始就过于拥挤的想法其实是一种错觉。

“This is something I was thinking about when I was interviewing Patrick. In some sense, when he started Stripe, payments was a super crowded industry. There’s PayPal, there’s obviously Visa, Mastercard. But, in another sense, there’s something strange in terms of domains you think of as crowded and totally competitive. There are usually totally obvious blind spots. 
“这是我采访帕特里克时一直在思考的事情。从某种意义上说，当他创立 Stripe 时，支付行业是一个超级拥挤的行业。有 PayPal，显然还有 Visa、Mastercard。但从另一个意义上说，在你想来是拥挤和完全竞争的领域，有些东西很奇怪。通常会有非常明显的盲点。

“In my case, it was just that I decided that I was going to spend a week preparing for a podcast episode instead of just a day. That doesn’t seem like it should have been the case. Similarly with Stripe, it was just ‘We’re going to make it easier for somebody to build an API for payments.’ It doesn’t seem like it should have been something PayPal missed. But in a strange sense, a lot of seemingly competitive domains are pretty easy to get a handle on.”
“在我这边，我只是决定我要花一周时间准备一集播客，而不是一天。这似乎不应该是这样。同样，对于 Stripe 来说，我们只是‘我们要让为支付构建 API 变得更简单。’这似乎不应该是什么 PayPal 会忽略的事情。但从某种奇怪的角度来看，很多看似竞争激烈的领域其实很容易掌握。”

There’s another key insight Patel shared from his talk with Collison. I ask him about his strategy in leading podcast episodes, specifically if he ever feels torn between a breadth-first and a depth-first approach — concepts borrowed from the two search algorithms that nearly every CS student learns at some point. How exactly does he grapple with the decision to either explore a wide range of topics superficially (breadth) or delve deeply into a few specific areas (depth)? Breadth has the advantage of appealing to a more general audience; for depth, it’s honoring the domain expertise of his guests.
帕特尔在与科利森交谈中还分享了一个关键见解。我问他关于主持播客节目的策略，具体是否曾在广度优先和深度优先方法之间犹豫不决——这两个概念借鉴于几乎每个计算机科学学生都学过的两种搜索算法。他究竟是如何处理探索广泛话题的表面层次（广度）或深入少数特定领域（深度）之间的决策？广度优先的优势在于能吸引更广泛的受众；而深度优先则是尊重他客人的领域专业知识。

On this, he goes back to Stripe and says “When you have an API that’s also responsible for payments, you need to make sure that it’s super reliable and secure. But you also need to be fascinating to other startups, which means you need to be deploying often. Stripe figured out how to do thousands of deploys a day on their API but also run an extremely reliable set of internal tests to make sure that they’re all secure.
在这点上，他回到 Stripe 并说“当你有一个既负责支付的 API 时，你需要确保它非常可靠和安全。但你还需要对其他初创公司有吸引力，这意味着你需要频繁部署。Stripe 找到了如何在他们的 API 上每天部署数千次，同时运行一套极其可靠的内部测试来确保所有内容都安全的方法。”

“In my case, people often say ‘Oh you can’t do as many episodes if you want to go deep.’ But you have to realize, at some point, that the Pareto Frontier is so far out there that you can just optimize for everything.”
“在我这边，人们常说‘如果你想深入探讨，就不能做那么多集。’但你必须明白，在某个时刻，帕累托前沿已经远得让你可以只专注于优化一切。”

A “Pareto Frontier” describes an optimal state in decision-making processes where you can’t improve one aspect without compromising another. Imagine a scenario where you’re trying to balance two competing objectives, like quality and cost. The Pareto Frontier represents the set of all points where you achieve the best possible balance between these objectives. It’s finding the sweet spot where you get the most quality for the least cost — and any move away from this point means you’ll either sacrifice quality or increase cost.
“帕累托前沿”描述了决策过程中的一种最优状态，即在不牺牲其他方面的情况下无法改进某一方面。想象一个需要平衡两个竞争目标的场景，比如质量和成本。帕累托前沿代表了在这些目标之间实现最佳平衡的所有点的集合。它是在找到那个能以最低成本获得最高质量的甜点位置——任何偏离这个点的举动都意味着要么牺牲质量，要么增加成本。

In the context of podcasting, as Patel refers to it, the Pareto Frontier would be the ideal balance between the number of episodes (breadth) and the depth of each episode. It’s about finding that point where you can produce a high quantity of episodes without sacrificing the in-depth exploration of each topic.
在播客的语境中，正如帕特尔所指出的，帕累托前沿就是集数数量（广度）和每集深度之间的理想平衡。它关乎找到那个可以大量制作播客，同时不牺牲每个主题深入探讨程度的位置。”

Except, as he has realized, in most cases, and especially his, “you are so far from the Pareto Frontier where you have to make that trade-off.”
然而，正如他所意识到的那样，在大多数情况下，尤其是对他而言，“你离帕累托前沿如此之远，以至于不得不做出这种权衡。”

The loyal listenership, the accolades from tech’s best leaders, the Substack response articles — it’s all impressive. But what Patel feels most proud of has little to do with it.
忠实的听众、来自科技界最佳领导者的赞誉、Substack 上的回应文章——这一切都令人印象深刻。但帕特尔最引以为傲的成就与此关系不大。

“There’s the big interviews and those go viral, everybody hears about them. But there are a few scholars who were not that well-known before I interviewed them. Sarah Paine is someone I interviewed recently, a historian and professor at the Naval War College. After she did the interview, her boss — the college president — was like ‘Oh my god, this is the biggest media thing that has happened to the Naval War College.’ I’m sure she got a bunch of cold emails after. Noah Smith even interviewed her because he liked that interview.”
“那些大型访谈会走红，每个人都会听到它们。但也有一些学者在我采访他们之前并不那么出名。我最近采访了莎拉·佩恩，她是海军战争学院的史学家和教授。在她接受采访后，她的老板——学院院长——说‘天啊，这是海军战争学院有史以来最大的媒体事件。’我确信她之后收到了很多冷邮件。诺亚·史密斯甚至因为喜欢那次访谈而采访了她。”

It’s a sign of the increasing credibility and influence of Patel’s work. (His episode with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei even happens to be part of the congressional record.)
这是帕特尔工作日益增加的信誉和影响力的标志。（他与 Anthropic CEO 达里奥·阿莫迪的访谈甚至恰好成为国会记录的一部分。）

Everything that is relevant to understanding society is relevant to understanding AI.
所有与社会理解相关的事物，都与理解人工智能相关。

While the podcast has grown to undisputable impact, there have been a couple of fans who were slower to recognize the credibility of Patel’s work: his parents. “They thought it was a total distraction. You know what’s funny? When Jeff Bezos said on Twitter, ‘You’re thoughtful and thought-provoking, please keep going,’ something like that, my parents were like, ‘Oh, that’s cool. You think you can talk to him about getting a job at Amazon?’” he remembers.
虽然播客已经产生了不可否认的影响力，但仍有一些粉丝较晚才认识到帕特尔工作的可信度：他的父母。“他们认为这完全是分心。你知道什么好笑吗？当杰夫·贝索斯在推特上说‘你深思熟虑且引人深思，请继续’之类的话时，我父母就那样说，‘哦，那很酷。你觉得你能和他谈谈在亚马逊找工作的机会吗？’”他回忆道。

Fortunately, after Patel’s interview with OpenAI Chief Scientist Ilya Sutskever, which has over a half million views on YouTube, his parents came around to supporting his work.
幸运的是，在帕特尔接受 OpenAI 首席科学家伊利亚·苏茨凯弗的采访后，该视频在 YouTube 上获得了超过五十万的观看量，他的父母最终支持了他的工作。

AI holds most of Patel’s focus and curiosity these days, serving as a thematic center that informs all his episodes — even those that draw heavily from other disciplines, like history or economics.
如今，人工智能占据着帕特尔的主要关注和好奇心，成为他所有节目的主题中心——即使那些大量借鉴其他学科（如历史或经济学）的节目也不例外。

“I think it has the potential to be the most important thing ever. There are so many different domains you have to understand to think about it because, in a sense, it’s like [creating] a new society. So everything that is relevant to understanding society is relevant to understanding AI.”
“我认为它有可能成为有史以来最重要的事情。要思考它，你必须了解许多不同的领域，因为从某种意义上说，它就像[创造]一个新社会。所以，所有与社会理解相关的东西都与理解人工智能相关。”

Though Patel has neither a Ph.D. in machine learning nor a position in tech policy, he isn’t afraid of the undertaking. He says “This is a common thing I’ve seen among high-agency young people: they get to meet the people who are supposed to be in charge, early on in their lives, and realize ‘Oh they’re just regular people. They seem competent but it doesn’t seem self-evident that they’ve got it handled.’ And sometimes it’s not fully handled.
尽管帕特尔既没有机器学习的博士学位，也没有科技政策方面的职位，但他并不害怕这项挑战。他说：“我经常看到高能动性的年轻人有这种情况：他们在年轻时有机会遇到那些本应负责的人，然后意识到‘哦，他们只是普通人。他们看起来很能干，但似乎并不明显地表明他们已经处理好了。’有时他们并没有完全处理好。”

“I’ve interviewed people where it seems like they haven’t necessarily thought about something as much as I would’ve hoped. Or I’ve gotten to a point where I’ve thought about a specific subtopic more than they have. That’s when you realize that you’re a part of the clique that’s supposed to do the thinking about it.”
“我采访过一些人，他们似乎并没有像我希望的那样深入思考某个问题。或者我已经到了一个阶段，对某个特定子话题的思考比他们更多。那时你就会意识到，你已经成为那个应该思考这个问题的群体中的一员。”

If Patel is right about AI changing society the way that he imagines — about how much it matters — then his podcast has the potential to matter just as much. It’s being listened to by at least some of the right people in power.
如果帕特尔关于人工智能以他想象的方式改变社会——关于其重要性的看法是正确的——那么他的播客也具有同等的重要性。它被权力体系中至少一些正确的人所收听。

Despite this information — or even pressure — he approaches his episodes in a more personal way. He refers to a quote by computer scientist Donald Knuth, ‘A program is written by an individual to be read by another human being, and it’s only incidentally true that computers can execute it,’ and says “Similarly, with podcasts, it’s really meant for me to learn from the person — both through all the preparation and the conversation — and only incidentally for the audience.”
尽管有这些信息——甚至压力——他仍然以更个人化的方式来处理他的节目。他引用了计算机科学家唐纳德·克努斯的语录，“一个程序是由个人编写的，供另一个人阅读，而计算机能够执行它只是偶然的真相，”并说“同样，播客确实是我从他人那里学习的工具——通过所有的准备和对话——而观众只是偶然的受众。”

When I ask him what he imagines his work might look like, in the future, in the new society he believes AI will create, he smiles.
当我问他想象他的工作在未来——在他相信人工智能将创造的新社会中——会是什么样子时，他微笑了。

“One of my friends put it this way, who’s an AI researcher himself. He said, ‘You were lucky enough to have the job that you would have in the post-singularity world anyways.’”
“我的一位朋友这样说过，他本人就是一位人工智能研究员。他说，‘你足够幸运，得到了一份你无论如何都会在奇点后世界拥有的工作。’”
